analysis.one_liner: Protects workers' early-retirement pension benefits when their employer is sold or merged.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote, dying in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company is sold, merged, or liquidated, workers sometimes keep their jobs but lose credit toward the subsidized early-retirement benefits their old pension plan promised, because the new employer runs a different plan or none at all. This bill would amend federal pension law (ERISA) and the tax code so that a worker's years of service under the successor employer count toward eligibility for the subsidized early-retirement benefit they had earned under the old plan, as long as the successor employer does not maintain that plan. In plain terms, a corporate restructuring could not be used to erase the early-retirement subsidy a worker had built up.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who stay on the job after their employer is acquired, merged, or liquidated but whose new employer does not continue the old pension plan. Without this change, they could lose their pro-rata share of a subsidized early-retirement benefit they had earned years of service toward; the bill guarantees those service years still count for eligibility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers whose employers are acquired or merged

how_it_helps.text: If an employer is sold, merged, consolidated, or liquidated and the successor employer does not continue the old pension plan, the worker's service with the successor employer must be counted toward eligibility for any subsidized early-retirement benefit under the old plan.
The protection is written into both ERISA (the federal private-pension law) and the Internal Revenue Code, closing off both the labor-law and tax-law routes around it.

analysis.who_pays: Acquiring employers and companies involved in mergers, acquisitions, and liquidations would carry the cost: they could not shed the early-retirement subsidy obligation by restructuring, and where relevant they would bear the pension accounting and funding consequences of honoring service credit across the transaction.
analysis.who_pays_short: Acquiring employers in mergers and acquisitions

drawbacks.text: The rule applies even where the successor employer deliberately keeps employees but runs its own different pension arrangement, which could discourage acquirers from taking on distressed divisions or add costs in mergers where workforce continuity was already planned.

The protection only covers eligibility for subsidized early-retirement benefits in successor-employer situations; it does nothing for workers whose plan is simply terminated or underfunded, so its reach is narrower than the general pension-security problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to affected workers is real and specific: a corporate sale or merger could no longer wipe out credit toward an early-retirement subsidy they had earned. The cost falls on acquiring employers, in the form of honoring service credit they did not directly accumulate, which is the point of the bill but is also a genuine compliance and funding burden in merger accounting. The bill is narrowly drafted, which limits both its help and its cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never acted on it, and the two-year Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on March 11, 2005.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, and no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 109th Congress.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that acquire, merge with, or liquidate other employers are better off, because they remain free to restructure without inheriting the old plan's subsidized early-retirement obligations. Workers who lose that credit in a restructuring are left with the law unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Majority party in the 109th Senate, controlling committee agendas and the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate during the 109th Congress and never brought the bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill with no cosponsors from either party, and the Republican-led Senate committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Acquiring employers and companies in mergers, acquisitions, and liquidations
industries.note: The bill would make successors in corporate transactions count former-plan service toward subsidized early-retirement eligibility instead of letting restructuring erase that credit, adding pension cost to deals. Its death leaves acquirers free to shed early-retirement subsidies through restructuring.

industries.industry: Sponsors of defined-benefit pension plans with early-retirement subsidies
industries.note: The bill leaves plan sponsors' existing discretion over whether to continue early-retirement subsidies through corporate transactions untouched. The status quo, in which a successor employer can drop the old plan and workers lose subsidy credit, is preserved.
